meta.title: Twelve Dots, Two on Every String
meta.summary: The major pentatonic is the triad plus two more notes per octave, and adding them turns every CAGED window into a regular twelve-dot box you already know how to hold.

spans.text: Chapter 2 promised the same five windows would keep filling in, and this is that promise landing again. Take the C form, the A form, any of the five you already know, and light two more notes inside each one — same window, same shape, just more of what was already there.
A major triad is three notes: the root, the third and the fifth —
. Add two more per octave, a
and a
, and you get five:
. In C that's
C D E G A
. That's the major pentatonic — the triad you already have, plus two notes. Define it that way and it stays honest: it's what those five notes add, never what some bigger scale is missing.
The full major scale has seven notes to the octave. This chapter's layer has five. Chapter 4 fills in the last two — not yet, and not here.
Here's what happens when you add the
and the

to any of the five windows: the dot count comes out exactly the same every time. Twelve dots. Two on every one of the six strings — no exceptions, no string left lopsided. Check it in any window you like, C form or A form or any other, and you'll find the same tidy count waiting.

That regularity is the whole point. Two notes on a string, sitting a fret or three apart, is one hand position with nothing to shift for. A triad window scattered seven or eight dots unevenly across six strings — some strings carrying two, some only one — which is part of why chapter 2 kept having to talk about pieces of a shape rather than the shape itself. A pentatonic window doesn't scatter. It fills in evenly, and that evenness is what turns a window into a box: something a hand can simply sit inside and play, top to bottom.

The twelve-dot count is the same everywhere, but it doesn't feel the same everywhere. Where the two new notes land, how far apart they sit, which pair of degrees ends up tripled inside a given window — all of that changes from form to form. That's what gives each of the next five lessons something real to teach, rather than the same box redrawn five times in five places.
One more thing worth restating before the windows start, in case you're arriving at this chapter after a gap.
caged-shape

draws every note of the window, not one grip a hand could hold. At the triad layer that meant more dots than five fingers could reach at once — the whole reason fragments existed. At this layer the same convention gives you the opposite result. Twelve dots spread across four frets is, in four of the five windows, roughly a hand's whole reach. The fifth, the D form, spreads wider than that, and its own lesson explains why.
Here's the fact this whole chapter is built on, and it's worth holding onto through every window that follows. Three of these five notes are the chord:

A player who only knows the box runs it up and down without ever landing anywhere in particular. That difference is what this chapter actually teaches — the shapes are already familiar; telling the chord tones from the rest is the new skill.
